strengths: Addresses an important and practical gap: existing image immunization methods (PhotoGuard, DAYN) require per-image optimization taking hours, which is impractical for large-scale deployment. The proposed feed-forward immunizer that learns a universal, prompt-agnostic perturbation via a single forward pass is a clear and useful contribution with dramatic speedups (0.07s vs 207-911s) and lower memory footprint.

First (to my knowledge) extension of image immunization to video content, which is a meaningfully novel application given the added computational burden of prior optimization-based methods; shows qualitative and quantitative (PSNR) improvement over naive baselines applied per-frame.

The two-stage end-to-end training framework (immunizer + differentiable editing loop with masked noise/edit losses) is a reasonable and clearly explained design, and the ablation on loss terms (Table 4) and loss weight alpha (Table 6) supports the design choices.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation including seen/unseen splits, quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, CLIP-T), a user study (67 participants) showing DiffVax ranked most effective at causing perceptible edit failure, robustness experiments against denoising/JPEG counter-attacks, and generalization tests to non-human objects and a second editing tool (InstructPix2Pix).

Reasonably transparent about limitations (per-editing-tool training requirement) and provides supplementary material with additional qualitative results, dataset/prompt construction details, and ablations.
weaknesses: The core technical idea (a learned/universal perturbation generator inspired by universal adversarial perturbations, applied to disrupt a fixed diffusion editing model) is somewhat incremental relative to prior immunization work and existing UAP literature; the main novelty is engineering the feed-forward pipeline and extension to video, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic insight.

The method requires training a separate immunizer per editing tool/model, which is a significant limitation for real-world deployment since attackers can choose from many editing tools; this is only lightly explored (two tools: SD inpainting, InstructPix2Pix) and no experiment tests cross-tool transfer (training on one editing tool and testing against a different one).

Robustness evaluation against counter-attacks is limited to only two simple defenses (a CNN denoiser and JPEG compression); more adaptive or adversarially-aware counter-attacks (e.g., an attacker aware of the immunizer's architecture, ensemble of transformations, or adversarial purification via diffusion) are not tested, so robustness claims may not generalize to a more determined adversary.

Quantitative results in Table 2 show DiffVax's degradation advantage (lower SSIM/PSNR/FSIM) is often modest relative to PhotoGuard-D, and the model is only second-best (not first) on SSIM(Noise) for unseen data with PhotoGuard-D having a small edge on imperceptibility in some cases — the gains are not uniformly dominant across all metrics.

The user study is relatively small-scale (67 participants, 20 image pairs) and focuses on 'unrealisticness' ranking without statistical significance testing, limiting the strength of the human-evaluation claims.

The video evaluation is very limited in scale (4 videos, 4 prompts, 64 frames), which is insufficient to strongly support claims of general effectiveness on 'in-the-wild' video content; also lacks a naive PhotoGuard-E or DAYN video baseline for more thorough comparison beyond PhotoGuard-D.

The paper does not analyze failure cases in depth (e.g., situations where DiffVax's noise fails to disrupt edits or where imperceptibility degrades), nor does it discuss the perturbation budget/constraint explicitly enforced during training (Eq. 1 defines a budget kappa but it is not clearly tied to the actual training loss or reported).

strengths: The core idea of replacing per-image gradient-based optimization (as in PhotoGuard/DAYN) with a feed-forward 'immunizer' network trained end-to-end is a sensible and practically valuable contribution, yielding a dramatic (claimed 250,000x) speedup and far lower GPU memory, which matters for large-scale deployment scenarios such as social media.
The paper is the first to extend diffusion-based image immunization to video content, which is a novel and relevant application direction, even if only demonstrated preliminarily.

The evaluation includes a reasonably broad set of qualitative examples (seen/unseen images, non-human objects, an alternate editing tool InstructPix2Pix, counter-attacks) plus a small human study, giving some multi-angle evidence for the method's behavior.
An ablation over the two loss terms and the loss weight hyperparameter is provided, lending some insight into the design choices.
weaknesses: The paper's central competitive claim is efficiency and robustness relative to DAYN (CVPR'24), the most relevant and recent baseline, yet DAYN is excluded from essentially all quantitative tables (Table 2 editing failure/imperceptibility, Table 3 video, Table 5 counter-attack robustness) — comparisons are made only against PhotoGuard variants and Random Noise. Table 1's claims about DAYN's lack of robustness and scalability are asserted rather than empirically verified in this paper's own experiments.

The method is trained and evaluated almost exclusively against a single editing model (SD v1.5 inpainting); the claimed 'universal'/model-agnostic generalization to other editing tools (e.g., InstructPix2Pix) is supported only by a handful of qualitative examples in the supplementary material with no quantitative metrics, undermining the generalization claims.

The video evaluation is extremely small-scale (4 videos × 4 prompts), which is insufficient to support the paper's emphasis on video protection as a key contribution; no robustness-to-counter-attack results are reported for video at all.

The counter-attack robustness analysis (Table 5) is limited to a denoiser and JPEG compression and compares only to PhotoGuard-D; it does not consider adaptive attacks that specifically target a known, fixed, feed-forward immunizer network (e.g., attacker fine-tuning a surrogate inversion/removal model), which is a natural and important threat model given that DiffVax is a fixed, publicly-describable function rather than a per-image optimized perturbation.

Some qualitative results (e.g., Fig. 1 'add sunglasses', Fig. 9 InstructPix2Pix results) show the edited-immunized output collapsing into large uniform/blank regions or extreme artifacts rather than a plausible failed edit, raising the question of whether the model has learned a somewhat degenerate 'erase-and-fail' behavior rather than a nuanced adversarial perturbation; this is not discussed or analyzed.

Dataset scale and diversity are modest: 1000 human images from a single clothing-focused dataset (CCP), with prompts synthesized by ChatGPT, and the evaluation is almost entirely human-centric; broader diversity (objects, scenes, varying resolutions) is relegated to a handful of supplementary examples without quantitative support.

The method still depends on an external SAM-based mask (for defining the target region), but there is no ablation or sensitivity analysis of how mask quality/availability affects immunization performance, nor discussion of the practical requirement that a user must have access to SAM-generated masks at protection time.

The reported superiority on SSIM(Noise) (imperceptibility of the pre-edit perturbation) over PhotoGuard-D is marginal and inconsistent (second place on seen split in Table 2), despite this being one of the two core desiderata of the method; the significance of this gap is not statistically tested.

strengths: Novel optimization-free formulation for image immunization against diffusion-based editing: a single trained immunizer performs immunization in a single forward pass (milliseconds) versus hours/days for prior optimization-based methods (PhotoGuard, DAYN), a substantial practical improvement for large-scale deployment.
First method to extend immunization to video content, with promising qualitative and quantitative (PSNR) results and much lower runtime than a naive PhotoGuard-style per-frame baseline.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation: quantitative comparisons on seen/unseen splits with multiple metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FSIM, SSIM-noise, CLIP-T), a human study on perceptual realism, an ablation on the two loss terms and the loss weight α, and robustness tests against two counter-attacks (denoising, JPEG compression).

Demonstrates generalization beyond the training distribution: unseen images, unseen prompts, non-human objects, and a different editing tool (InstructPix2Pix), supporting the claim of a generalizable universal perturbation.

Clear writing, useful comparison table (Table 1) situating the contribution relative to prior work, and supplementary material with additional qualitative results and dataset/prompt construction details that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: DAYN, described as a key related work and included in the qualitative comparison table (Table 1), is not included in the main quantitative comparison (Table 2/3/5); only Random Noise, PhotoGuard-E, and PhotoGuard-D are used as quantitative baselines, weakening the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claims.

Robustness evaluation is limited to two relatively simple, non-adaptive counter-attacks (a CNN denoiser and JPEG compression); there is no evaluation against an adaptive/white-box attacker who has knowledge of the immunizer model itself, which is an important threat model for a learned, fixed-weight defense (unlike per-image optimized noise, a single trained immunizer could in principle be more vulnerable to a targeted adaptive attack once its weights or behavior are known).

Video evaluation is very small-scale (4 videos, 4 prompts, 64 frames), limiting confidence in the generality of the video results; no human study or SSIM/FSIM/CLIP-T metrics are reported for video, only PSNR.

The method requires separate training per editing tool (acknowledged as a limitation), which somewhat undercuts the 'universal immunizer' framing, since a real-world adversary could simply switch editing tools/pipelines to bypass a given trained immunizer.

The core metrics (SSIM/PSNR/FSIM degradation between edited-immunized and edited-clean images) measure how much the edit output is corrupted, but do not clearly distinguish between 'edit meaningfully blocked' versus 'output simply destroyed/garbled' (e.g., some qualitative results show near-uniform gray/noisy outputs rather than a graceful failure); this could conflate immunization efficacy with a degenerate failure mode of the editing model, and is not carefully discussed.

The human study is relatively small (67 participants, 20 image pairs) and reports only an aggregate 'unrealisticness' ranking across methods, which conflates imperceptibility of noise on the clean image with disruption quality of the edited image; separate perceptual studies for these two distinct objectives would be more informative.

Dataset for training/testing (1000 CCP images, largely human-centric, single-person full/close-up shots) is relatively narrow; broader content diversity (e.g., complex scenes, multiple subjects) is not tested, and the training data source (CCP) and prompts (ChatGPT-generated) may not reflect the diversity of real-world adversarial editing prompts.
